newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa development bank status changes refused.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa development bank status changes refused.

text.p: South Africa's parliamentary finance committee on Wednesday refused to approve a bill aimed at giving an apartheid-era development bank legal status and turn it into a company.

Instead, it asked the Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) and state finance department to resolve differences about the planned change with interested parties and report back as soon as possible.
If these differences could not be resolved, public hearings would be held, possibly on March 10.

Finance Department director-general Maria Ramos told Reuters that the delay in passing the bill would have no effect on government support for DBSA, which taps about one billion rand from the financial market each year to fund infrastructural project.
The rejection of the bill followed objections by committee members and financial organisations that DBSA was not being turned into a bank and that all the interested parties had not been consulted.
They were concerned that it could pose unfair competition to commercial banks and other government financial institutions.

Formed in 1983 through a treaty between the white South African government and its former nomially independent black homelands, DBSA was thrown into a legal limbo by the adoption of a new constitution after the country's first democratic elections in 1994.

DBSA chief executive Ian Goldin told the committee on Tuesday that the bill would give the bank legal status and provide it with a share capital of five billion rand, of which two billion rand would be held by government.
This would help the bank retain its Triple A rating in the face of the withdrawal of government guarantees and allow it to continue to provide low interest loans to high risk infrastructure projects.
Ramos admitted that the bill had only been published on January 24 and that some interested parties might not have time to study it.

Following legal advice it had been decided that it would be best to convert the bank into a company as it would not be a deposit-taking institution but would raise funds in the market for infrastructural projects that other banks regarded as too risky to support.
